content: The SL-LPA (second-line line-probe assay) should only be utilized for testing specimens from patients with confirmed multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB). The adoption of SL-LPAs does not negate the necessity for conventional culture and drug susceptibility testing (DST) capabilities. While SL-LPAs demonstrate good specificity in detecting resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectable drugs (SLIDs), culture and phenotypic DST remain essential to definitively rule out resistance to these drug classes and other second-line drugs. SL-LPAs cannot determine resistance to individual drugs within the fluoroquinolone class. Resistance-conferring mutations detected by SL-LPAs are strongly correlated with phenotypic resistance to ofloxacin and levofloxacin. However, certain mutations, such as the eis C14T mutation, are associated with resistance to specific drugs within a class, such as kanamycin resistance in strains from Eastern Europe. SL-LPAs are suitable for direct testing of sputum specimens, regardless of whether the samples are smear-negative or smear-positive. These assays are designed to detect tuberculosis and resistance to fluoroquinolones and SLIDs from sputum samples. However, their performance on other sample types, such as bronchoalveolar lavage, gastric aspirates, or extrapulmonary samples (e.g., tissue samples, cerebrospinal fluid, or other body fluids), has not been adequately evaluated. Culture and phenotypic DST play a critical role in monitoring a patient’s response to treatment and detecting additional resistance to second-line drugs during treatment. SL-LPAs are best suited for use in central or national reference laboratories, but they can also be implemented at the regional level if the necessary infrastructure, including three separate rooms, is available. All patients identified by SL-LPAs should have access to appropriate treatment and ancillary medications. Research priorities include improving the understanding of the correlation between resistance-conferring mutations detected by SL-LPAs and phenotypic DST results, as well as patient outcomes. Further studies are needed to better understand the relationship between specific mutations detected by SL-LPAs and the minimum inhibitory concentrations of individual drugs within the fluoroquinolone and SLID classes. Additionally, the detection limits of SL-LPAs for identifying heteroresistance should be determined. More evidence is required to assess the impact of SL-LPAs on appropriate MDR-TB treatment initiation and mortality. Future studies should adhere to the STARD (Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies) guidelines to improve reporting quality. Country-specific cost-effectiveness and cost-benefit analyses of SL-LPA implementation in different programmatic settings are also encouraged. Pyrazinamide (PZA) is a critical antibiotic for treating both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB due to its unique ability to eradicate persistent bacilli and its synergistic properties with other antibiotics. While monoresistance to PZA is rare, resistance to PZA is strongly associated with MDR/RR-TB, with an estimated 30–60% of MDR/RR-TB cases also resistant to PZA. Therefore, detecting PZA resistance in patients diagnosed with RR-TB is essential to guide clinicians in deciding whether to include or exclude PZA in the treatment regimen. High-complexity reverse hybridization-based nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) may be used to diagnose PZA resistance on patient isolates. However, these tests require appropriate infrastructure and skilled personnel. For patients with bacteriologically confirmed TB, high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs may be used on Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) culture isolates to detect PZA resistance instead of culture-based phenotypic DST. This is particularly relevant for populations such as children, people living with HIV, and those with extrapulmonary TB, as the test is recommended for use on culture isolates. The GenoScholar™ PZA-TB assay, developed by Nipro (Osaka, Japan), is a commercially available rapid molecular test for detecting PZA resistance. Unlike other line-probe assays (LPAs) such as MTBDRplus and MTBDRsl, the GenoScholar PZA-TB assay does not include specific mutant probes because resistance mutations are distributed across the entire pncA gene without predominant mutations. Instead, the assay targets a 700-base pair fragment covering the entire pncA gene and promoter region up to nucleotide -18 of the wild-type H37Rv reference strain. The GenoScholar PZA-TB assay could potentially be implemented for routine care to diagnose PZA resistance. However, limited data have been published on its diagnostic accuracy. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to collate available data on the diagnostic accuracy of the PZA LPA assay for detecting PZA resistance in TB patients, aiming to guide policymakers and clinicians. The WHO Global TB Programme initiated an update of the current guidelines and commissioned a systematic review on the use of high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs for detecting PZA resistance in individuals with TB symptoms. Two PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions were formulated to guide the evidence search and analysis: 1. Should high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs on sputum be used to diagnose PZA resistance in patients with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary TB, irrespective of rifampicin resistance, compared to culture-based phenotypic DST or a composite reference standard? 2. Should high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs on isolates be used to diagnose PZA resistance in patients with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary TB, irrespective of rifampicin resistance, compared to culture-based phenotypic DST? The systematic review identified three studies (122 participants) for PICO 1 and seven studies (964 participants) for PICO 2. The evidence for PICO 1 was insufficient to draw conclusions about the diagnostic accuracy of NAATs on sputum. For PICO 2, the studies demonstrated a wide range of sensitivity (36–100%) and specificity (96–100%) for detecting PZA resistance. However, the evidence was downgraded due to selection bias, indirectness, and inconsistency, resulting in very low certainty for sensitivity and low certainty for specificity. Cost-effectiveness analyses of high-complexity reverse hybridization-based NAATs were also reviewed. No published studies specifically assessed the costs or cost-effectiveness of the GenoScholar PZA-TB assay. Indirect evidence from other LPAs suggests that operational costs often exceed test kit costs. The GenoScholar PZA-TB assay costs approximately $16 per test kit, with equipment costs around $14,000. Further reductions in test costs are anticipated with global distribution.
